description: Hello, this is our team and we're looking forward to challenge ourselves, collaborate and have fun at NASA's space app challenge!
summary:
Mars: REDSHIFT is an interactive, browser-based space mission design game created by Team Astro Builders for the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge.

The player takes the role of a rookie systems engineer and works through three missions: a low-Earth-orbit climate CubeSat, a Mars water-ice orbiter, and an exoplanet telescope at Sun–Earth L2.

For each mission, players select spacecraft systems, scientific instruments, an orbit, and a launch vehicle while balancing budget, mass, power, battery capacity, data, communications, and mission lifetime. They then launch their design into a 3D flight simulation, respond to mission anomalies, and see how their decisions affect the outcome.

A debrief gives a mission grade and explains what worked or failed, with the option to revise the design and try again.

Our goal is to make space mission engineering easier to understand through hands-on experimentation instead of a lecture or a static quiz.
details:
What does the project do?

Mars: REDSHIFT is a single-player space mission design game where players experience the decision-making process behind planning and operating a spacecraft.

Instead of simply giving players information about space missions, we put them in the position of a rookie systems engineer working in a Mission Design Lab. They are given a scientific objective and have to figure out how to build a spacecraft capable of achieving it with limited resources.

The game currently contains three missions with increasing complexity:

  1. LEO Climate CubeSat: Design a small satellite to study greenhouse gases and atmospheric conditions from Low Earth Orbit. Players learn about spacecraft mass limits, solar power, battery capacity, eclipses, and communication constraints.
  2. Mars Water-Ice Orbiter (Mars: REDSHIFT): Design an orbiter capable of searching for buried water ice on Mars. This introduces more demanding decisions involving deep-space radiation, solar flares, dust storms, high-data scientific instruments, and long-distance communications.
  3. L2 Exoplanet Telescope: Design a space telescope operating around Sun–Earth L2. Players must consider infrared instruments, thermal protection, sunshields, spacecraft lifetime, and the challenge of returning large amounts of scientific data.

How does it work?

Each mission follows four main stages.

1. Mission Briefing

Players are introduced to the mission through short visual-novel-style conversations with two characters: Mission Director Vance and Dr. Lin, the lead scientist.

They explain why the mission matters and introduce some of the engineering challenges. Before entering the spacecraft builder, players also choose a mission priority: either focusing on maximum scientific value or taking a safer, more cost-efficient approach.

2. Spacecraft Design

This is where most of the engineering decisions happen.

Players build their spacecraft through seven categories:

  • Frame
  • Power
  • Engine and avionics
  • Radio and communications
  • Scientific instruments
  • Orbit
  • Launch vehicle

Every selection affects other parts of the mission. For example, choosing a more powerful scientific instrument might increase scientific value, but it can also increase spacecraft mass, power consumption, and the amount of data that needs to be transmitted.

The game recalculates the engineering constraints immediately and displays six live indicators:

  • Budget
  • Spacecraft mass versus rocket capacity
  • Power generation and consumption
  • Data transmission
  • Battery capacity during eclipses
  • Mission lifetime

There are also launch compatibility checks. A spacecraft cannot launch if it exceeds the budget, weighs too much for the selected rocket and orbit, lacks sufficient power, or fails other essential requirements.

The spacecraft also has an interactive 3D Hangar preview. Players can rotate their design, inspect its components, and change its hull colour.

3. Launch and Orbital Simulation

Once the design passes the launch checks, players launch their spacecraft into a 3D simulation.

The simulation shows the spacecraft travelling towards its destination and entering its operational orbit. Players can switch between normal and double speed.

During the mission, the game models sunlight, eclipses, battery consumption, scientific data generation, and communication windows with ground stations.

Players also encounter mission anomalies. Examples include solar flares, battery shortages during eclipses, Mars dust storms, and communication bottlenecks.

Their responses depend partly on the hardware they selected earlier. For example, a radiation-hardened flight engine unlocks a safer response to solar flares, while reserve batteries and high-gain antennas provide additional options during emergencies.

This creates a direct connection between spacecraft design and mission performance.

4. Mission Report and Improvement

After the simulation, players receive a mission report with a grade ranging from S to Failed.

The report evaluates four areas:

  • Science Value: 35%
  • Data Return: 30%
  • Resource Margin: 20%
  • Cost Efficiency: 15%

More importantly, the game explains why certain decisions helped or harmed the mission. Instead of only displaying a score, it identifies problems and suggests which spacecraft components or subsystems should be improved.

Players can select "Revise Design" and return directly to the builder without losing their previous selections.

The idea is simple: failure should teach players something, not just tell them they lost.

What benefits does it have?

The main benefit is that it makes interconnected engineering concepts easier to understand.

In real mission design, spacecraft systems cannot be considered independently. A decision involving scientific instruments can affect power requirements, total mass, communication capacity, launch costs, and even mission lifetime.

We wanted players to experience these relationships themselves.

It also introduces players to different types of space missions, from relatively small Earth-observation satellites to interplanetary orbiters and deep-space telescopes.

The experience is designed for beginner to intermediate learners, so players do not need an aerospace engineering background to get started.

Another advantage is accessibility. The application runs entirely in the browser, requires no installation or account, and does not depend on external API calls or backend servers. Campaign progress is saved locally.

What is the intended impact?

We hope Mars: REDSHIFT makes more students and space enthusiasts interested in the engineering behind space exploration.

People often see the final result of a space mission, such as a satellite image or a discovery from Mars, without understanding how many engineering decisions were required to make that result possible.

We want players to understand that a successful space mission is not simply about building the most powerful spacecraft. It is about making sensible compromises, managing limited resources, understanding risks, and choosing the right equipment for the mission objective.

We also want to show that engineering failure is a useful part of the learning process. Players can experiment with different designs, observe what goes wrong, and improve their next attempt.

What tools, programming languages, and technologies were used?

We developed the project using:

  • React 19: Building the user interface and managing application state.
  • TypeScript 5.7: Implementing the game logic, mission data structures, and resource calculations.
  • Three.js 0.174: Creating the interactive 3D spacecraft models, planetary environments, and orbital visualizations.
  • Vite 6: Development server and production build system.
  • HTML, CSS, and SVG: Building the interface, character portraits, and visual elements.
  • GLSL: Creating a custom atmospheric lighting shader.
  • Web Audio API: Generating the background soundtrack, launch effects, alerts, and interface sounds directly in the browser.
  • Canvas API: Generating procedural planetary textures.
  • Node.js and npm: Managing dependencies, running automated tests, and building the application.
  • GitHub Actions and GitHub Pages: Automating the testing, production build, and website deployment.

We also used Google Antigravity as an agentic coding environment during development.

The application does not require specialised physical hardware, sensors, or external data services.

How is the project creative?

We wanted to avoid creating another educational project that simply presents information through slides, text, or multiple-choice questions.

Our approach combines a visual-novel-style story, spacecraft design, resource management, and an interactive orbital simulation into one experience.

One of the features we are particularly interested in is the relationship between hardware selection and emergency decisions.

For instance, players who prepare for radiation exposure by selecting the appropriate equipment get access to better options when a solar flare occurs. Players who ignore those requirements may suffer damage or lose scientific data.

This makes earlier decisions matter later in the mission.

We also created procedural 3D spacecraft models that change according to the player's selected components, custom character portraits, planetary textures, and an original soundtrack generated through the Web Audio API.

Rather than relying on a collection of external visual and audio assets, much of the visual and audio experience is created directly through our own code.

What factors did the team consider?

We considered several things while developing the game.

Accessibility and learning curve: The target audience includes beginners and younger students. We avoided overwhelming players with complicated technical terminology and added plain-English explanations, warnings, and character guidance.

Scientific credibility: We used NASA publications and educational resources to inform the mission concepts and engineering relationships. We also clearly separate NASA references from simulated gameplay values.

Engineering trade-offs: We wanted every meaningful upgrade to have consequences. A stronger instrument should not simply be a free improvement; it should introduce new demands on other spacecraft systems.

Development time and technical scope: We had a very limited development period. We therefore focused on delivering a complete playable experience rather than attempting multiplayer functionality or an overly complicated spacecraft CAD editor.

Accessibility features: We included keyboard navigation, a reduced-motion option, sound controls, and a 2D fallback for the orbital visualization when WebGL is unavailable or reduced motion is enabled.

Reliability: We kept the application client-side, using local mission data instead of relying on live APIs or backend services that could fail during a judging session.

The project was developed by Team Astro Builders. I worked on development and presentation, Maji Hkawn Jan managed the project and vision, Han Nyein Zin and Hein Say Paing Soe helped with playtesting, and Thant Thiri Nwe supported research and pitching.

Our main objective was to make a complete, enjoyable, and educational mission-design experience within the time available.
